Selected work
Video automation

Raw footage cut down with no human editor.

Transcribe, let a model decide which segments are dead air or a bad take, cut them, then burn right-to-left Arabic captions and the brand on.

  • Groq whisper-large-v3
  • LLM cut layer
  • ffmpeg
  • RTL caption burn-in
42% Dead air removed in one prototype test Where this number comes from

The problem

An ed-tech content creator was spending more time cutting silence, filler and restarts out of recordings than making them. It is the most mechanical work in video and the least automatable by traditional tools, because deciding whether a pause is dead air or a deliberate beat is a judgement, not a threshold.

What it does

01

Hears the footage properly

Transcription runs on a large speech model, so Arabic and code-switched speech come back accurate enough to cut against.

02

Decides, rather than thresholds

A language model reads the transcript with its timings and marks what to remove: dead air, filler, false starts and abandoned takes. A silence-detector cannot tell a bad take from a pause for effect.

03

Cuts and rebuilds

The edit list is applied with ffmpeg, then right-to-left Arabic captions are burned in correctly and the brand treatment is stitched on.

How it is built

TranscribeJudge cutsCutCaptionBrand

A CLI rather than a service, so it runs on the operator's own machine with their own keys and nothing leaves it. Brand theming is one config file, which is what lets the same pipeline serve more than one client without a fork.

What I'd watch if it were yours

The judgement layer is the product

Transcription and cutting are commodities. What is worth paying for is the part that decides, and that is the part a threshold cannot do.

Right-to-left captions are their own problem

Arabic text has to be shaped and ordered correctly before it is burned into pixels. Getting this wrong is invisible to a non-reader and immediately disqualifying to a reader.

Measure against real footage

The prototype test used an ed-tech creator’s footage with permission.

One prototype test on an ed-tech creator’s footage recorded 42% dead-air removal.
